prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Gradually, Into, What

outputs.L1:
Gradually, a girl’s innocence itself becomes her major crime.

A doe and her two fawns bent low in the sumac along the bank of a highway, the pinched peach of their ears twitching in the heat.

Into the disordered evening, my brother cut out only his face from every photograph in the hall, carefully slipping each frame back into position.

What good does it do? Decades of no faces other than our own chipping faces. What good does it do, this resemblance to nothing we know of the dollhouse?

New parents watch their newborn resting in a sunny patch of an empty room, the newborn making sense of its container—

And from the road, a deer ripened in death, and a tuft of fur—or dandelion—tumbled along, gently circled: driftwood, shaking loose, gathered, dissolving into the mouths of jewelweed nearby.

Earth is rife with iron, and blood is rich in stardust.

Immediately, I spotted one hoof print, then nothing, as if this was where she dragged herself out of the body.

Strips of tire torn from their orbit.

Is it right, then, that we are left to hurtle alone?
outputs.L2:
Little by little, a girl’s own purity turns into the gravest accusation against her.

Beside the highway, in the sumac on the embankment, a doe lowered herself with her two fawns, their narrow, peach-colored ears flickering in the heat.

In the unsettled dusk, my brother went through the photographs in the hallway and removed only his own face from each one, then slid every frame carefully back into its place.

What does that accomplish?

Years pass with no faces left except ours, faces wearing away.

What is gained by this likeness to nothing we recognize in the dollhouse?

New parents stand watching their infant lie in a bright square of sunlight in an otherwise empty room, the baby beginning to understand the shape that holds it—

And out by the road, a deer had grown swollen in death, while a small clump of fur—or perhaps a dandelion—rolled past, turned softly in circles, like driftwood coming loose, collecting, then breaking apart into the mouths of nearby jewelweed.

The earth is full of iron, and blood carries the dust of stars.

At once I saw a single hoof mark, and then no more, as though that was the place where she had pulled herself free of the body.

Shredded bands of tire, ripped from their circular path.

So is it true, then, that we are abandoned to go speeding forward by ourselves?
outputs.L3:
The text presents innocence not as something protected, but as something that is slowly redefined and punished. A girl’s innocence appears at first as natural and unguarded, yet the world around her begins to treat it with suspicion. What should be seen as vulnerability becomes interpreted almost as guilt, as though simply existing in a state of openness makes her responsible for the harm or judgment directed toward her. In this way, the text suggests that innocence can be distorted by social forces until it resembles a crime.

This concern with vulnerability is deepened through the speaker’s reflections on family, memory, and erasure. The image of a brother cutting his own face out of photographs is especially powerful. Photographs usually preserve family history, offering proof that someone was present and belonged to a shared past. By removing his face, the brother symbolically removes himself from that history. His act suggests shame, disappearance, or a desire to escape being remembered. At the same time, it damages the family’s memory as a whole, leaving behind gaps where a person should be. The speaker is therefore not only remembering the past, but also confronting the ways in which memory can be altered, wounded, or made incomplete.

The natural world in the text is similarly marked by fragility and violence. Images of deer, death, and roadside debris create an atmosphere in which beauty and destruction exist side by side. Deer often suggest gentleness, innocence, and grace, but when placed near images of death or the roadside, they become symbols of how easily life can be broken. Roadside debris further emphasizes this sense of damage, suggesting the aftermath of movement, collision, and neglect. Nature is not presented as peaceful or separate from human violence; instead, it is shown as vulnerable to the same forces of harm and decay.

The text also expands its focus beyond individual suffering by connecting the body to the material world. References to human blood, earth, iron, and stardust suggest that living beings share a common origin with the planet and even the cosmos. Blood contains iron; iron comes from ancient stars; the body returns to the earth. These connections make human life seem both intimate and vast. The speaker places personal and familial pain within a larger material cycle, implying that humans are not separate from nature but made of the same substances as everything around them.

By the end, the text arrives at a haunting question about solitude. If all living beings share the same physical origins, then there is a possibility of deep connection. Yet the final lines seem to ask whether that connection is enough. Despite common blood, shared matter, and a shared world, each creature may still be left to move through existence alone. The text therefore holds two ideas in tension: that all life is materially connected, and that emotional or existential loneliness may remain unavoidable. Its final effect is one of uncertainty, fragility, and quiet grief.
outputs.L4:
The text unfolds as a meditation on innocence, familial erasure, mortality, and dislocation, presenting these themes through a series of fragmented, image-rich scenes. Deer appear not only as animals but as emblems of vulnerability and fleeting grace, moving through the landscape with a quietness that mirrors the speaker’s own sense of disappearance. Photographs evoke the unstable nature of memory: they preserve faces and moments, yet also expose how easily a family history can become incomplete, blurred, or erased. Images of infancy deepen this tension, suggesting a time before language and identity fully form, when the self is dependent, unprotected, and only partially remembered by others.

Throughout the text, death intrudes in stark and ordinary ways, especially through the image of roadside death. The road becomes a place of passage and violence, where bodies can be displaced, struck, or abandoned. This setting connects personal grief to a wider, indifferent world. Mortality is not treated as a single dramatic event but as something woven into the landscape, appearing in animals, family traces, and the fragile body of the child. The natural world absorbs these losses without explanation, making grief feel both intimate and vast.

The fragmented structure reinforces the speaker’s emotional dislocation. Rather than offering a clear narrative, the text moves through broken images and associations, as if trauma has disrupted ordinary time. Family, memory, and selfhood do not remain stable; they dissolve into deer, snow, roads, photographs, and silence. In this way, private suffering becomes cosmic, connected to the cycles of nature and death, yet it also remains profoundly isolating. The speaker’s loss is everywhere reflected in the world, but that reflection does not necessarily bring comfort. Instead, the text suggests that identity is fragile, that family can vanish from memory or record, and that grief often leaves the self suspended between human connection and the vast impersonality of the natural world.
outputs.L5:
**Gradually Into What**

Gradually, we move through life without always knowing exactly where we are going. Each choice, each lesson, and each challenge leads us into something new. Sometimes the future feels uncertain, and we ask ourselves, “What comes next?” But even when the answer is unclear, progress still happens step by step.

Change does not always arrive suddenly. It often grows quietly, turning small efforts into meaningful results. What matters most is the willingness to keep moving forward, even when the path is not fully visible. Gradually, we become stronger, wiser, and more prepared for whatever life brings.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single-paragraph prose poem in a contemporary lyric style about girlhood, family photographs, deer by a highway, birth, death, and cosmic loneliness; avoid clear narrative closure.
counterfactuals.output: In the shoebox of family photographs every girl is a small weather system, bangs cut crooked, knees silvered with playground dust, held up to the sun by hands that will later vanish into hospital sheets, into steering wheels, into the ordinary dark behind the eyes; there is my mother before she was my mother, standing in a yard like someone listening for her own name to arrive from the future, and there I am, or almost am, a blood-bright rumor under her dress, a star not yet tired of burning. At dusk the deer gather by the highway, tender machines of hunger, their bodies pausing at the edge of our speed, and I think of birth as that same bright hesitation, the world rushing past in both directions while someone pushes you toward it, saying breathe, saying girl, saying nothing that can save you. In one photograph my grandfather’s thumb blurs the corner, a pink eclipse over the picnic table, the deviled eggs, the cousins with their mouths open mid-laugh; in another, the dead are still alive because light once touched them and could not stop touching them. I used to believe family meant a circle, but it is more like a constellation drawn by a child who has never seen the actual sky: lines invented between distances, names pinned to burning absences, the little animal heart crossing and crossing the road. Somewhere a baby is being lifted wet into the air; somewhere a body is cooling under a clean white sheet; somewhere the universe expands without looking back, and the girls in the photographs keep smiling as if they have just been told a secret, as if the flash were another planet calling them home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental poem that feels like fragmented memories: a brother cutting his face out of family photos, newborn parents in an empty sunny room, roadkill deer, iron, blood, stardust, and the question of whether we are alone.
counterfactuals.output:
In the shoebox:  
mother’s hand on my shoulder,  
father blurred by afternoon,  
and where my brother was—  
a clean white wound.

He took scissors to himself  
again and again,  
left only the lake behind him,  
the picnic blanket,  
the birthday cake bending under candles,  
our smiles holding space  
for a face-shaped silence.

*

Before I was born  
my parents were newborn too.

They stood in an empty sunny room  
with dust turning gold around them,  
no crib yet, no bills,  
no history in the walls.

Just two people  
blinking in the light,  
soft-skulled with hope,  
learning the names  
of future griefs.

*

On the highway shoulder:  
a deer folded into itself,  
brown altar,  
flies stitching the air.

Its open body said  
red, red, red,  
as if the world had a language  
under the fur.

Iron in the blood.  
Iron in the star.  
Iron in the pan on the stove  
where my mother cooked dinner  
after the accident,  
after the phone call,  
after every ordinary apocalypse.

*

We are mostly aftermath.

A little salt.  
A little carbon.  
A little stardust  
caught in the mouth  
saying brother, saying stay,  
saying why did you make yourself  
a hole in every year we had.

The universe expands  
like a family  
after someone leaves the table.

Chairs glow with absence.  
Windows fill with sun.  
The dust keeps orbiting.

*

At night I ask the ceiling  
if we are alone.

The ceiling says nothing.

The deer says nothing.

The photographs say less.

But somewhere  
inside the blood’s dark factory,  
iron remembers fire.

Somewhere  
my brother’s missing face  
keeps shining from the floor  
in small cut moons.

Somewhere  
two newborn parents  
stand in a room  
before anyone has vanished,

and the light touches them  
as if answering  
yes,

no,

yes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, surreal literary passage with no line breaks, blending images of innocence becoming guilt, animals near a road, damaged family resemblance, a dollhouse, and a final existential question.
counterfactuals.output: The child stood at the shoulder of the road with jam on her hands and a halo of gnats, watching the lambs nose the ditch as if searching for the lost white buttons of their own innocence, while beyond them a fox, flattened into a red rumor, seemed still to be listening for permission to die; in the back seat, her brother slept with their father’s mouth on his face, a damaged inheritance, the family resemblance cracked like a mirror carried through a storm, and their mother kept saying no one had done anything, no one was to blame, though the dollhouse in the trunk rattled with every mile, its tiny rooms overturned, its nursery blackened, its miniature father nailed upside down to the painted kitchen wall; by dusk the girl understood that guilt was not an act but a weather, entering through the skin, turning milk sour in the cup and making even the horses in the field lower their heads like witnesses, and when the moon rose over the road, thin as a fingernail clipping, she opened the dollhouse door and found inside a smaller road, a smaller ditch, a smaller child with jam-dark hands looking back at her, already guilty, already beloved, and who, if anyone, was dreaming whom?
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a poem in the style of a modern American poetry journal submission—elliptical, image-heavy, and unsettling—using motifs of deer, highways, childhood innocence, family erasure, and cosmic matter.
counterfactuals.output:
**No One Taught the Deer to Pray**

At the edge of the highway, a deer  
wears the headlights like a second skull.

All night the asphalt keeps arriving  
from somewhere behind us.

My brother says stars are just holes  
where the dead look through,  
but my brother is not in the photographs anymore.

Mother cut him out with sewing scissors.  
Father burned the negatives in a coffee can.  
The smoke went up pure and instructional.

We were children then,  
which is to say we believed anything  
that bled could be forgiven.

In the ditch, milkweed opened  
its soft green fists.  
A radio tower blinked its red eye  
over the soybean fields.

The deer did not move.  
Its body was a question  
the car answered incorrectly.

Later, I found a tooth in the carpet  
and kept it in a matchbox with my fossils—  
small moons of what had lived before language.

At dinner, no one said accident.  
No one said antlers.  
No one said the name that made the walls  
lean closer.

Outside, the sky kept making more of itself:  
dark matter, dust, the old extravagance  
of hydrogen becoming light.

I pressed my palm to the window  
and watched my reflection disappear  
into the glass.

Somewhere, a highway divided a forest  
with the confidence of a knife.

Somewhere, the deer stepped out again,  
tender and exact,

as if innocence were not a pasture  
but the moment before impact,

as if every family were a constellation  
missing its most necessary star,

as if erasure were only another word  
for distance.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an avant-garde prose poem that moves associatively from a girl’s innocence to a doe and fawns, a brother removing his face from photos, a newborn in sunlight, a dead deer, hoofprints, tire strips, and a closing question about isolation.
counterfactuals.output:
The girl keeps her innocence in a blue cup by the sink,  
rinsing it each morning until it shines with the rumor of sky.  

She walks to the edge of the field where the grass loosens its green hair,  
and there—without ceremony—a doe lifts her head,  
two fawns trembling beside her like commas the world has not yet finished.  
Their ears are soft doors. Their eyes carry the weather before it happens.  

Somewhere, her brother is cutting himself out of photographs.  
Not with scissors, exactly—  
with absence, with thumbprints, with the slow chemical refusal  
to remain a son in the family album.  
In every picture he leaves behind a white oval,  
a ghost-shine where the face should explain the body.  

Then the newborn arrives, slick and astonished,  
laid in a patch of sunlight on the bed.  
The light touches the scalp first,  
then the tiny fists, closed around nothing,  
as if nothing were a treasure that could be lost.  

By evening, the road has given back a deer.  
Not the doe, maybe. Not the fawns.  
But a deer, broken into stillness,  
its flank dark with the grammar of impact.  
The girl stands where the shoulder crumbles into weeds  
and sees hoofprints in the mud—  
small urgent signatures going everywhere and nowhere.  

Beside them, tire strips blacken the asphalt,  
long burnt ribbons,  
proof that something tried to stop  
after it had already become motion.  

And the brother’s missing face keeps shining in the album.  
And the newborn keeps drinking sunlight through closed eyes.  
And the fawns keep stepping, stepping, into the uncut field.  

Tell me: when every creature leaves a mark to say it was here,  
what is it called when no one follows?
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
